claims.claim: Agriculture is the cultivation of crops and the raising of livestock; geographers commonly divide farming into subsistence agriculture (growing food mainly to sustain the farmer and household, consuming most of it and staying outside the cash economy) and commercial agriculture (producing primarily for sale and profit).

The First (Neolithic) Agricultural Revolution began roughly 10,000-12,000 years ago, when humans domesticated plants and animals in several regions independently, allowing people to become sedentary and form villages.

Domestication clustered in a limited number of culture hearths, including the Middle East and Southwest Asia, Mesoamerica and the Andes, Northeast India, North China, and East Africa; it was not spread evenly across the globe.

The Second Agricultural Revolution coincided with the Industrial Revolution; mechanization (tractors, combines, the internal-combustion engine), the railroad, and new farming techniques generated the food surpluses needed to feed workers in factories and moved agriculture beyond subsistence, marking the birth of commercial agriculture.

The Green Revolution of the mid-20th century introduced higher-yielding grain varieties of wheat, corn, and rice together with fertilizers, pesticides, irrigation, and new machinery; its spread across South, Southeast, and East Asia and Mexico greatly increased food supply and helped countries such as India become self-sufficient in basic foods.

Norman Borlaug is the name most linked to the Green Revolution: working in Mexico in the 1940s and 1950s he developed a robust dwarf wheat that made Mexico self-sufficient in wheat by 1956, then introduced it to India and Pakistan in the mid-1960s, and he received the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize.

The Green Revolution is credited with large yield gains and reduced hunger, but it is also critiqued for dependence on fertilizers, pesticides, and heavy irrigation, for environmental costs, and for uneven benefits; agriculture accounts for roughly 70% of global freshwater withdrawals, one concrete measure of that resource intensity.

Shifting cultivation (slash-and-burn) is an extensive form of subsistence agriculture in which farmers clear and burn vegetation to make a plot (a swidden), cultivate it for a few years until soil fertility declines, then abandon it and move on; it supports only low population densities and is common in tropical rainforests.

Pastoral nomadism is an extensive form of subsistence agriculture based on herding domesticated animals across arid and semi-arid grasslands, deserts, steppes, and high plateaus, moving to find water and pasture rather than planting crops; nomadic pastoralists occupy roughly a fifth of Earth's land area.

Intensive agriculture maximizes output per unit of land through heavy inputs of labor or capital on small parcels (for example wet-rice farming in monsoon Asia), while extensive agriculture spreads lower inputs over large areas (for example ranching or shifting cultivation); the two are ends of a spectrum, not opposites tied to development level.

Johann Heinrich von Thünen (1783-1850) set out a model of agricultural land use in the first book of Der isolierte Staat (The Isolated State), 1826: around a single central market, land use falls into concentric rings determined by transport cost and perishability, with intensive perishable production (dairy, market gardening) nearest the market and extensive uses (grain, then livestock ranching) farther out.

In von Thünen's classic scheme the innermost ring is dairying and market gardening (perishable, must reach market fast), the next is forest/wood (heavy and bulky, costly to move), then grain and field crops (lighter and storable, so grown farther out), and the outermost ring is livestock ranching on cheap distant land where animals can be walked to market.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many 'agricultural revolutions' there are and how they are numbered
positions: Many human-geography texts name three: the Neolithic/First, the Second (Industrial-era), and the Green Revolution (sometimes called a Third).
Some sources add a later 'biorevolution' or genetic-engineering phase after the Green Revolution.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as three dated milestones (Neolithic, Second/Industrial, Green Revolution) matching the assignment scope, with the later biotechnology phase named only in passing and handed to other topics.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What crops sit in von Thünen's middle rings
positions: The 1826 model placed forest/firewood in a ring close to the city because wood was heavy and essential fuel.
Modern retellings sometimes compress or relabel the rings and treat firewood as less central.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Reported the classic four-ring order (dairy/market gardening, forest, grain, ranching) and framed it as a model whose specific goods are dated even though its logic of transport cost and perishability endures.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft was generic boilerplate ('agriculture is a foundational concept students use to organize information') with no substantive claim about subsistence vs commercial farming, the agricultural revolutions, farming types, or the von Thünen model; none of it was usable as evidence.

Attributed the Green Revolution's dwarf wheat to Norman Borlaug and the land-use model to Johann Heinrich von Thünen (1826), as required.

sourceRecords.title: Von Thunen Model of Agricultural Land Use: An Overview
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Supports: von Thunen (1783-1850) as a farmer/landowner/economist who created an early spatial economic model in the first book of The Isolated State (1826); the model's six assumptions (single central city in an isolated region surrounded by wilderness, flat terrain, uniform soil/climate, cart transport, profit-maximizing farmers); and the four concentric rings in order (1 dairy/intensive perishable farming nearest the market; 2 forestry/wood, heavy and bulky; 3 grain, lighter and less perishable, extensive; 4 livestock ranching outermost, animals driven to market). Reference-only secondary source; facts restated in original prose.
